nodes.date_label: After Imperialism (1965) · Cultural Internationalism and World Order (1997) · Global Community (2002)

nodes.label: David Brion Davis
nodes.date_label: The Problem of Slavery in Western Culture (1966) · The Problem of Slavery in the Age of Revolution (1975) · Inhuman Bondage (2006)
nodes.description: Historian of slavery and abolition whose comparative intellectual history treated bondage as central to Western and Atlantic modernity. In his2008 retrospective,Davis asks how moral perception and organized opinion changed while slavery remained economically powerful. His interpretation gives ideas a major role in abolition; that emphasis,and his assessment of enslaved revolt,remain arguments rather than a settled hierarchy of causes.

nodes.label: Gary Gerstle
nodes.date_label: Working-Class Americanism (1989) · American Crucible (2001) · The Rise and Fall of the Neoliberal Order (2022)
nodes.description: Historian of American labour,political economy and national belonging. Gerstle’s concept of a political order explains how a dominant movement can require opponents to accept its basic terms. His account of neoliberalism links bipartisan political settlement to capitalism’s globalization and later crises,while leaving the form of a successor order open. Earlier work connects labour and nationalism rather than assuming patriotic language is inherently conservative.

nodes.date_label: Decisive Encounters (2003) · The Global Cold War (2005) · The Cold War:A World History (2017)

nodes.label: Gordon S. Wood
nodes.date_label: The Creation of the American Republic (1969) · Empire of Liberty (2009) · Power and Liberty (2021)
nodes.description: Historian of the American Revolution whose account joins republican ideas to changes in social authority. In an interview published posthumously in2026,Wood contrasts monarchical patronage with popular sovereignty and traces competing notions of representation. His interpretation of revolutionary transformation is influential and contested; broad claims of democratic modernity do not erase slavery or unequal inclusion.

nodes.label: Edmund S Morgan
nodes.date_label: The Stamp Act Crisis (with Helen M.Morgan) (1953) · American Slavery,American Freedom (1975) · Inventing the People (1988)
nodes.description: Historian of early America who made the relation between slavery and freedom a central interpretive problem. In his1972 address,Morgan rejects treating enslavement as an exception to the national story or freedom as mere disguise. His Virginia-centered argument asks how racial domination and the independence claimed by white colonists developed together. Its particular mechanism remains open to debate rather than explaining every colonial society.

nodes.label: Michel Vovelle
nodes.date_label: Piété baroque et déchristianisation en Provence (1973) · Idéologies et mentalités (1982) · La Mentalité révolutionnaire (article) (1991)
nodes.description: Historian of collective mentalities and the French Revolution who connected long changes in death and religion to moments of political rupture. In La Mentalité révolutionnaire,Vovelle asks whether slow transformations can accelerate in revolutionary crisis. His analysis treats hope and fear,violence and fraternity as interrelated,and explicitly rejects both unconditional devotion to the Revolution and blanket denunciation.

nodes.label: Drew Gilpin Faust
nodes.date_label: A Sacred Circle (1977) · Mothers of Invention (1996) · This Republic of Suffering (2008)
nodes.description: Historian of the American South whose writing links slavery,women’s wartime choices and the cultural consequences of mass death. Faust’s interview with Jim Leach explains how slaveholders’ records can reveal enslaved family ties and how Confederate women’s exhaustion changed their relation to war. Her biographical work uses an individual life to investigate social structures while preserving the distinction between understanding and endorsement.

edges.evidence_note: Own2008 pp252–253 and265–266; Western cultural focus and contested weighting of revolt remain limits,not universal coverage.

edges.evidence_note: Own2022 opening definition and New Deal/neoliberal comparison; historical model rather than a fixed law or inevitable sequence.

edges.relationship: Gerstle links neoliberal ascendancy and breakdown to political choices,globalization and crises of market legitimacy.

edges.evidence_note: Own2017 HKS transcript; temporal reach to nineteenth-century ideologies is distinguished from a simple extension of every Cold War event.

edges.relationship: Westad investigates how postwar superpower interventions intersected with anticolonial change beyond Europe.
edges.evidence_note: Own2005 chapter4 public opening specifies US perceptions,anti-communism and intervention capacity; this is a contribution to colonial/postcolonial history,not automatic membership in a theoretical school.

edges.relationship: Wood reconstructs popular sovereignty and representation as contested transformations in revolutionary political thought.
edges.evidence_note: Own Massari interview answers on sovereignty and virtual/actual representation; published after death,recording not misdated.

edges.relationship: Wood connects republican transformation to changes in patronage,deference and social dependence.
edges.evidence_note: Own interview opening on monarchy as a social hierarchy; his transformative thesis is attributed and does not establish equal freedom for all.

edges.relationship: Morgan’s American paradox connects revolutionary commitments to independence with the simultaneous development of slaveholding society.
edges.evidence_note: Own1972 pp5–8 rejects both simple hypocrisy and a story that treats slavery as an exception; Virginia-centered mechanism is bounded.

edges.relationship: Morgan places racial domination within the formation of colonial freedom and social independence.
edges.evidence_note: Own1972 pp5–8 explicitly recognizes racism while asking about the material/social conditions of independence; not a universal account of every colony.

edges.relationship: Vovelle relates long-duration collective mentalities to the rapid transformations of revolutionary crisis.
edges.evidence_note: Own1991/2012 opening explicitly engages Mandrou and Braudel; not a claim that all Annales historians shared his revolutionary interpretation.

edges.relationship: Vovelle analyzes revolutionary hope and fear as related collective forces rather than isolated psychological traits.
edges.evidence_note: Own pp234–235 discussion of Lefebvre’s paired concepts; a specific earlier resource for emotion history,not sole foundation or later professional self-identification.

edges.relationship: Faust treats slaveholding women’s changing wartime interests as consequential for Confederate endurance and collapse.
edges.evidence_note: Own2011Leach answer on exhaustion and family/property preservation; scoped to slaveholding women rather than all Southern women.

edges.relationship: Faust’s Hammond biography uses an individual’s extensive records to investigate slavery and social power in the Old South.
edges.evidence_note: Own2011answers explain biography as a window onto society and reconstruct enslaved kinship from records; understanding the subject does not endorse his values.
